newsitem.title: USA: Trucks increase U.S. death risk for car occupants.
newsitem.headline: Trucks increase U.S. death risk for car occupants.

text.p: A surge in the number of light trucks that are growing heavier each year is increasing the risk of death for those sharing the road, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced Tuesday in a report summarizing six studies.
In accidents between cars and light trucks, including pickups, vans and sport-utility vehicles, 80 percent of the fatalities were occupants of the cars, one report showed.

The NHTSA findings are of increasing importance due to the rapid increase in sales of heavier, larger vehicles, said Robert Eichler, President of Technical Services, an automobile accident forensic consulting company.
"Essentially, when the big guy runs into the little guy, the little guy is always worse off," Eichler said. "It's a matter of physics."
Light trucks accounted for 44 percent of all new vehicles sold last year, automakers reported. Ford said it sold more light trucks last year than passenger cars.

Not only are more light trucks hitting the roads, they are getting heavier. Between 1985 and 1993, the average truck gained 340 pounds. Light trucks, on average, weigh 900 pounds more than passenger cars, NHTSA said.
An increase in the weight of light trucks makes them more dangerous, the NHTSA said.
The NHTSA study found that the fatal crash rate decreases 0.3 percent for every 100-pound reduction from a light truck. The injury crash rate decreased 1.3 percent for every 100 pounds shed.
A 100-pound reduction in the weight of light trucks could prevent 40 deaths and 601 injuries each year, the NHTSA said.

But many who buy light trucks choose them because they want the added safety associated with the heavier vehicles, said Barry Felrice, director of regulatory affairs at American Automobile Manufacturers Association.
"If you take weight out, you would take away some of the safety added to those vehicles," Felrice said. "Would you want to ride in a lighter weight vehicle and put your family at risk?"
